Hollow Tiles: Why That Tapping Sound Matters

It is not a cosmetic complaint. Here is what causes hollow tiles, why they fail, and why patching over them makes it worse.

18 Jun 20265 min readGO XPERT SOLUTION

Tap across a tiled floor and most tiles return a solid, dull sound. Then some return a distinctly hollow one. That difference is not in your imagination — it means there is a void between the tile and the screed beneath it.

What causes it

  • Adhesive applied in spots instead of full coverage
  • Adhesive left too long before the tile was laid
  • Dusty or poorly prepared screed surface
  • Rushed work near the end of a construction programme

Why it fails eventually

A tile bonded across its full area shares load with the screed. A tile sitting over a void does not — it flexes. Add furniture, foot traffic and thermal movement, and the tile cracks, lifts at the edges, or the grout line opens up.

In wet areas it is worse: water enters through the open grout, sits in the void, and eventually finds its way to the unit below.

A hollow tile is not a defect because of how it sounds. It is a defect because of what it will become.

The wrong fix

Laying new tiles over debonded ones is one of the most expensive mistakes we see. It adds weight to a bond that is already failing, and when it lets go, both layers come up — doubling the removal cost.

The correct approach

  • Tap-test to map the full extent of the hollow area, not just the tile you noticed
  • Remove the debonded tiles completely
  • Prepare the screed surface properly
  • Re-lay with correct adhesive coverage across the whole tile

If your unit is still within its DLP, this is the developer's responsibility. Have the extent mapped and documented before you accept any partial repair.
